question: How is 'a messenger' connected syntactically to the preceding words?

positions.position: An omitted verb such as 'He makes/sends him' governs the accusative.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī cites poetic ellipsis; Abū Ḥayyān prefers this as the least strained parse; al-Samīn illustrates implied verbs with poetry and 59:9. Versions supply makes, sends, or recites.

positions.position: It means that Jesus speaks to the people as a messenger.
positions.reasons: Al-Zajjāj and Abū Isḥāq prefer this because the following first-person declaration is his speech; the Kufans let rasūl carry the sense of saying.

positions.position: It coordinates with earlier circumstantial descriptions or the clause 'He teaches him'.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya connects it with Jesus's honor or speech as child/adult; Ibn ʿĀshūr treats yaʿlamuhu as a single circumstantial clause. Abū Ḥayyān objects to long separation in some parses. Al-Samīn reports the Sheikh rejecting the long-link analysis as built on another weak coordination.

positions.position: It is circumstantial after 'He teaches him', treating wāw as extra.
positions.reasons: Al-Akhfash proposes an extra wāw; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn call this unsupported or weak.

positions.position: It is governed by an implied 'I was sent' inside Jesus's quoted speech.
positions.reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī supplies both speech and verb to resolve the person shift; Abū Ḥayyān says the double omission is needless, while al-Samīn explains its logic.

positions.position: As a verbal noun 'message', it is another object of 'teach him'.
positions.reasons: Al-Ḥūfī and Abū al-Baqāʾ propose this; al-Samīn adduces poetry. Al-Ālūsī objects that Arabic does not use 'teach a message' this way.

turns_on: Whether a governing verb is supplied, the phrase coordinates with earlier predicates or circumstances, or rasūl is taken as a verbal noun.

question: What does rasūlan mean here?

positions.position: A sent messenger, Jesus.
positions.reasons: Al-Samīn derives the adjective on faʿūl and compares ṣabūr and shakūr; al-Ālūsī says this is the immediate sense.

positions.position: A message, as a verbal noun.
positions.reasons: Al-Samīn cites two anonymous poetic lines; Abū al-Baqāʾ allows it, but al-Ālūsī rejects it as less natural.

turns_on: Whether rasūl names a sent person or a message.

question: How is rasūlan read?

positions.position: The usual accusative rasūlan.
positions.reasons: The accusative supports an omitted governing verb or circumstantial parse.

positions.position: A variant reads rasūl in the genitive, coordinated with 'a word'.
positions.reasons: Al-Yazīdī is named; Abū Ḥayyān finds the long separation weak, and al-Samīn awkward but finds no clearer parse.

turns_on: The case ending changes its syntactic link.

question: When did Jesus become a messenger?

positions.position: Revelation or commission came in adulthood at thirty, followed by three years of prophecy.
positions.reasons: Wahb and al-Baḥr report age thirty; al-Ālūsī calls that account famous. One report instead gives three months and three days before his raising.

positions.position: He was commissioned in childhood, in one account at age three.
positions.reasons: Al-Baghawī reports the childhood view; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī points to Jesus speaking as an infant and 19:29–30.

positions.position: His preaching lasted thirty-three years.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṣādiq's report gives thirty-three years; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī suggests the figure may refer to his lifespan.

turns_on: The reports give incompatible ages and durations.

question: To whom was Jesus sent, and how broad was his mission?

positions.position: His commission was to all the Children of Israel.
positions.reasons: Jishumī, al-Ṭabrisī, Rāzī and Kur'an Yolu explicitly oppose the claim that he addressed only a particular Israelite group.

positions.position: He was sent only to a particular Israelite group.
positions.reasons: Some Jews are said to claim this; Bayḍāwī gives a limited-commission possibility.

positions.position: The wording rebuts a claim that Jesus was sent to non-Israelites.
positions.reasons: Bayḍāwī and an unattributed report offer this; al-Ālūsī doubts the alleged Jewish claim, finding it absent from familiar Jewish books.

positions.position: His special messenger mission was to Israel, while prophethood could reach other peoples.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes particular messengership from conveying religion generally; he cites Moses's address to Pharaoh and Jesus's acceptance among Romans, eastern peoples, and Najrān.

turns_on: Whether all Israel, only a subset, or a particular mission within wider prophethood.

question: How does Jesus's Israelite mission relate to Torah law?

positions.position: He confirmed and taught Torah law while making some prohibitions lawful.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya mentions certain foods, camel meat, fish and birds; al-Qushayrī and Jishumī say some rulings were retained and some abrogated.

turns_on: Retaining earlier law with some abrogation.

question: Who was the first and last prophet of Israel in the reports?

positions.position: Joseph was first and Jesus last.
positions.reasons: Al-Baghawī asserts this; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī report it.

positions.position: Moses was first and Jesus last.
positions.reasons: A report attributed to the Prophet in Jishumī says this; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī also note Moses as an alternative.

turns_on: Reports differ between Joseph and Moses for the first.

question: What minor vocal or sound variants occur in the opening words?

positions.position: The hamza of Isrāʾīl and the first-person suffix have dialectal variants without changed sense.
positions.reasons: Qirāʾāt ER records both the base pronoun vocalization and a dialectal suffix variant, plus a change in the glottal stop of Isrāʾīl.

question: Whose speech is 'I have come to you' and how does it enter the narrative?

positions.position: The angels tell Mary what Jesus will later say to Israel.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān carry the announcement onward; the transition to Jesus's speech is understood after 'Israel'.

positions.position: The narrative shifts to Jesus's later direct address to Israel.
positions.reasons: Asad prefers this on the narrative movement from 3:52; al-Ṭabrisī says Jesus addressed them when sent.

turns_on: Where angelic announcement ends and Jesus's later speech begins.

question: How is the first annī in 'I have come' read and governed?

positions.position: With fatḥa, it depends on messengerhood or an implied bi or li.
positions.reasons: Al-Kisāʾī relates it to sending; Sībawayh and al-Farrāʾ delete bi; al-Naḥḥās treats anna as accusative; Ibn ʿĀshūr hears the declaration accompanying the mission.

positions.position: A kasra reading begins direct speech or a fresh assertion.
positions.reasons: Al-Zajjāj and Ibn Khālawayh allow an implied saying or new sentence; Qirāʾāt ER describes the independent assertion.

turns_on: Open hamza attaches the clause; broken hamza resumes or quotes speech.

question: What does 'a sign' denote here, and why is it singular?

positions.position: It is proof of Jesus's prophethood and truthful mission, embracing the listed miracles.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Isḥāq, Rāzī and others call it evidence; al-Baghawī says many signs establish one truth; al-Ālūsī says indefiniteness magnifies it; Rāzī treats the singular as generic.

positions.position: The singular sign is specifically the clay bird; later cures form a new sentence.
positions.reasons: Al-Wāḥidī explicitly parses the bird miracle as the sign and the other wonders as subsequent discourse.

turns_on: Whether it names bird-making specifically or a class/unity of multiple miracles.

question: Is 'sign' read in the singular or plural?

positions.position: The common text has singular āya in both occurrences.
positions.reasons: Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn take singular as a collective or generic designation.

positions.position: Ibn Masʿūd or ʿAbd Allāh reads plural āyāt in both places.
positions.reasons: This directly reflects the multiple signs.

turns_on: The canonical singular is generic; Ibn Masʿūd's plural expresses the number of acts.

question: How does 'with a sign' attach to 'I have come'?

positions.position: It attaches to 'I have come', with bāʾ marking accompaniment or transitivity.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī gives both uses; Ibn ʿĀshūr emphasizes Jesus's status as messenger while taking the bāʾ as accompaniment.

positions.position: It is a circumstantial phrase: Jesus came bearing a sign.
positions.reasons: Al-Samīn allows an omitted general predicate, but rejects Abū al-Baqāʾ's specific implied 'advancing'.

turns_on: Whether a direct complement or a circumstantial accompaniment.

question: How does the following 'to make lawful' clause relate to 'I came with a sign'?

positions.position: It is coordinated with Jesus's coming: he came with a sign and to make some things lawful.
positions.reasons: Al-Kashshāf links the following wa-li-uḥilla back to bi-āyatin min rabbikum.

question: What does 'from your Lord' modify, and why say 'your Lord'?

positions.position: It attaches to 'I have come': Jesus came from God with the sign.
positions.reasons: Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī allow this; al-Biqāʿī and al-Ālūsī say 'your Lord' evokes beneficence and obedience.

positions.position: It qualifies the sign as having its figurative origin with God.
positions.reasons: Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn posit an omitted relational phrase; al-Ālūsī calls min figurative origin.

turns_on: Whether it qualifies the sign or the coming.

question: Why does the speech shift between singular and plural address?

positions.position: The shift shows the sign is witnessed and beneficial both individually and collectively.
positions.reasons: Al-Biqāʿī says it answers doubts that only a group could witness it or that it benefits just one person.

question: How is 'that I create' read and parsed?

positions.position: Kasra: it is an independent assertion or explanatory quotation of the sign.
positions.reasons: Nāfiʿ is commonly named, with Abū Jaʿfar added by Ibn ʿĀshūr and the two Medinans by Ibn al-Jazarī; al-Wāḥidī, al-Ṭabrisī and Rāzī prefer the explanatory link, citing 5:9, 3:59 or 48:29.

positions.position: Fatḥa: the clause apposes the first annī or the sign, or predicates an omitted 'it is'.
positions.reasons: Al-Fārisī reports all but Nāfiʿ opening it; grammarians variously make it accusative, genitive, or nominative. Abū al-Baqāʾ also supplies 'I mean'.

turns_on: Fatḥa subordinates the explanatory clause; kasra can resume it or explain the sign.

question: What does 'I create' mean in Jesus's claim?

positions.position: Jesus measures and shapes existing clay into a bird likeness.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī's successors cite craft usage, Zuhayr and other poetry, a measured sandal, and 29:17 and 23:14 for nonabsolute uses. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls proportioning the root sense and distinguishes originating an animal.

positions.position: Khalq can also mean bringing an entity from nonexistence, a sense reserved for God.
positions.reasons: Abū Ḥayyān distinguishes the two senses; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says bodily origination properly belongs to God, while figurative khalq covers fabricating falsehood at 29:17.

turns_on: Whether khalq here is shaping measured material or origination from nonexistence.

question: Can a human be called a creator or originator on the evidence of this verse?

positions.position: A servant can be called creator only in a qualified sense of forming or originating an act; God alone is Creator absolutely.
positions.reasons: Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī use the verse against the Mujbira; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 'best of creators' at 23:14. Ibn ʿAṭiyya distinguishes Jesus's shaping from God's origination of life.

positions.position: The divine name al-Khāliq belongs only to God.
positions.reasons: Rāzī reports his school's appeal to 13:16 and 35:3, while he rejects treating 35:3 alone as decisive because its negation includes providing from heaven.

positions.position: Al-Khāliq is not literally a divine name if it implies conjectural measuring.
positions.reasons: Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Baṣrī advances this objection; Rāzī's school answers that measuring can mean knowledge without conjecture.

turns_on: The scope of human agency and the divine name al-Khāliq.

question: Was the bird miracle requested by challengers?

positions.position: The Israelites challenged Jesus to make a bat.
positions.reasons: Reports say they called other miracles magic, selected the hardest bird, then still called him a sorcerer.

positions.position: He offered the sign himself while a schoolboy; it was not demanded.
positions.reasons: Ibn Isḥāq says the boys doubted his offer and spread the news to their teacher. Abū Ḥayyān finds no demand apparent from the verse.

turns_on: Public demand versus an offered sign at school.

question: When did Jesus first animate the clay bird?

positions.position: As a boy in a scribal school.
positions.reasons: Ibn Isḥāq says the other boys witnessed it, publicized it, and Mary later fled.

positions.position: After he claimed prophethood, as a challenge from the Israelites.
positions.reasons: Rāzī, al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī report the request for a bat.

turns_on: Schoolboy story versus challenge upon claiming prophethood.

question: What other grammatical scope and ordering details are noted in the miracle clauses?

positions.position: The coordinated healing and revival clauses remain within the scope of annī and its predicates.
positions.reasons: Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī state their syntactic dependence.

positions.position: The imperfect verbs portray repeated acts and are ordered from the greatest creative sign through healing, revival, and disclosure.
positions.reasons: Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn emphasize recurring action; Abū Ḥayyān identifies creation as the foremost miracle.

question: Why does Jesus say 'for you'?

positions.position: The shaping serves the audience's benefit by inviting faith and ending denial.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says it qualifies his limited shaping; al-Samīn calls the lām purposive, and al-Bursawī specifies faith as the purpose.

question: What is the clay and what does 'from clay' contribute?

positions.position: It is ordinary clay, water and earth that can receive a shape; min marks its starting material.
positions.reasons: Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī cite sealing a document or coating a house; al-Ḥarālī describes matured water and earth. Abū Ḥayyān says the source material excludes ex nihilo creation; al-Samīn rejects a merely explanatory min.

turns_on: Its physical sense and whether min limits the material source.

question: What does the clay-bird miracle show beyond Jesus's truthfulness?

positions.position: It displays God's power to create life and resurrect whatever He wills.
positions.reasons: Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmits Ibn Isḥāq; al-Biqāʿī says power over some dead proves power over all and compares Adam.

positions.position: It parallels Jesus's own unusual birth, which should not suggest his divinity.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī links it to the fatherless birth; al-Biqāʿī says Adam's dust creation is still more astonishing.

turns_on: The notes give distinct emphases on divine life, resurrection, Adam, and Jesus's birth.

question: What minor lexical and grammatical details accompany the bird narrative?

positions.position: The result becomes a living bird, while the clay term has related Arabic forms and names.
positions.reasons: Abū Ḥayyān notes the transmitter nicknamed Muṭīn; al-Samīn says ilā Banī Isrāʾīl can depend on rasūl or be its omitted adjective. The bird is truly living, as al-Kashshāf explains.

question: How does the comparison 'like the form' work syntactically?

positions.position: Kāf or its phrase modifies an omitted object: Jesus makes something shaped like a bird.
positions.reasons: Most grammarians and al-Samīn favor this; Ibn ʿĀshūr takes the object from 'I create'.

positions.position: Kāf itself is a noun meaning 'likeness' and direct object.
positions.reasons: Al-Akhfash and Abū al-Ḥasan permit this; al-Samīn says other grammarians restrict a noun-like kāf to necessity.

positions.position: Kāf modifies an omitted verbal noun: I create a creation like a bird's form.
positions.reasons: Abū ʿAlī proposes this; al-Samīn objects that the challenge concerns the created result, unless the verbal noun means its object.

turns_on: Whether kāf is a noun object, modifies an omitted object, or modifies an omitted verbal noun.

question: What does hayʾa mean here?

positions.position: The prepared visible shape or configuration of a bird.
positions.reasons: Al-Zajjāj and al-Baghawī derive it from preparation or setting right; al-Ḥarālī describes the arrangement of limbs; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it a clay image.

positions.position: A verbal noun transferred to the thing prepared.
positions.reasons: Al-Samīn compares khalq for a created thing; al-Ālūsī contrasts the verbal-noun analysis with a noun of state or a boundary-defined quality.

turns_on: Whether a state, form, or verbal noun for its formed result.

question: How is hayʾa read and pronounced?

positions.position: A variant eases hamza to a doubled yāʾ, hayya.
positions.reasons: Al-Zuhrī, Abū Jaʿfar, al-Aʿraj and others are named across reports; al-Samīn calls it eloquent, while Qirāʾāt ER notes no semantic change.

positions.position: The common reading retains hamza after the silent yāʾ.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it the reading of all readers; some accounts distinguish the main text from al-Zuhrī and Abū Jaʿfar's eased form.

turns_on: Hamza retained versus its vowel transferred to a doubled yāʾ.

question: What bird did Jesus fashion, and what happened to it?

positions.position: He fashioned a bat, presented as the hardest or most remarkable bird.
positions.reasons: Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Isḥāq say people chose it because it is flesh without feathers; later reports add teeth, breasts, ears, live birth, milk, menstruation, laughter, and twilight vision. Some say he made no other kind.

positions.position: The bird flew while watched, then fell dead out of sight.
positions.reasons: Wahb's report distinguishes Jesus's craft from God's unmediated, enduring creation. Some place the episode at school, others amid challengers.

positions.position: The clay likeness became a living flying bird like other birds.
positions.reasons: Al-Kashshāf, Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī stress that the resulting bird truly flew by God's leave.

positions.position: He fashioned multiple birds or several kinds.
positions.reasons: The plural reading and repeated action support this for al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī and others; al-Ālūsī reports this against the bat-only view.

turns_on: Bat only versus several birds, and whether it died after leaving view.

question: What does al-ṭayr mean, and how is it read in 'form of the bird'?

positions.position: The common al-ṭayr is a collective bird species, usable for one or many.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī calls it plural of ṭāʾir; Abū al-Ḥasan and Sībawayh call it collective, with regular plurals aṭyār and ṭuyūr. Al-Akhfash treats it as plural like rukb.

positions.position: Abū Jaʿfar and others read singular al-ṭāʾir, naming one bird or a genus.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabrisī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya say the first singular can be generic; al-Nashr says Abū Jaʿfar uses it in both places and notes hamza transmission.

positions.position: Ṭayr can also mean flying itself or, by usage, destiny or fortune.
positions.reasons: Asad cites 7:131, 27:47, 36:19 and 17:13, supporting his parabolic reading of the bird sign.

turns_on: Collective ṭayr versus singular active participle ṭāʾir, and the lexical scope of ṭayr.

question: What is the blowing, and what can it act upon grammatically?

positions.position: Nafkh is forcefully expelling air or breath into the fashioned figure.
positions.reasons: Jishumī defines air from the mouth; al-Ḥarālī says forceful sending from its source; al-Nābigha's poetic construction can omit fī.

positions.position: The breath indicates spirit as a subtle, windlike body.
positions.reasons: Jishumī and some theologians infer this from the wording; Rāzī compares Gabriel's breath into Mary.

turns_on: Ordinary breath through the mouth versus theological inference about spirit; preposition retained or deleted.

question: Are there other readings of 'I breathe into it'?

positions.position: The ordinary reading has masculine fīhi.
positions.reasons: Its antecedent can be the formed thing, a bird, or clay; 5:110 uses feminine agreement with hayʾa.

positions.position: A rare reading has fa-anfukh-hā without fī.
positions.reasons: Al-Farrāʾ transmits it, al-Kashshāf attributes it to ʿAbd Allāh; the feminine refers to hayʾa. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Samīn cite Arabic and poetry for direct-object nafkh.

turns_on: Masculine with fī versus feminine direct object.

question: What does the verse imply about Jesus's own bodily actions?

positions.position: Blowing is truly attributed to Jesus as a servant, while God grants life.
positions.reasons: Jishumī uses the attribution as evidence that servants act; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says Jesus's modeling and breath connect him visibly to the sign.

question: What does the pronoun in 'into it' refer to?

positions.position: The concrete bird-like object or form implied by the comparison.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī calls it the bird; al-Ālūsī takes hayʾa by sense as the thing formed, explaining masculine here and feminine at 5:110. Ibn ʿĀshūr points to an omitted object. Al-Zamakhsharī treats kāf as noun-like; Ibn Hishām objects to that grammar.

positions.position: The particular shaped clay, not clay in general.
positions.reasons: Al-Zajjāj, al-Thaʿlabī, Rāzī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya allow clay; al-Wāḥidī objects to generic clay, while al-Samīn answers that min can select a portion.

positions.position: The created result implied by 'I create'.
positions.reasons: Abū ʿAlī and al-Samīn offer a verbal-noun or created-object antecedent.

turns_on: A shaped object implied by the comparison versus the clay, bird, form, or act of creation.

question: How is the resulting bird read, and how does yakūn work?

positions.position: Nāfiʿ, Yaʿqūb and Abū Jaʿfar read ṭāʾiran: each formed thing becomes one flying bird.
positions.reasons: The singular can refer to a single species or distribute over each creation, as 24:4 gives eighty lashes to each. Al-Nashr distinguishes Abū Jaʿfar's singular in both places; Qirāʾāt ER says the participle stresses flying.

positions.position: The common ṭayran is collective: one or many birds become real birds.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī favors it for repeated acts, muṣḥaf spelling and transmission; al-Samīn favors matching first ṭayr and written form. Kāna is preferably incomplete with ṭayran predicate.

positions.position: Yakūn can be complete, with ṭayran/ṭāʾiran circumstantial.
positions.reasons: Abū al-Baqāʾ permits it; al-Samīn calls the bare species noun awkward circumstantially and rejects equating complete kāna with 'became'.

positions.position: A variant has feminine takūn, agreeing with the fashioned form.
positions.reasons: Al-Mufaḍḍal is named for this reading.

turns_on: Collective ṭayran versus singular ṭāʾiran, with complete or incomplete yakūn.

question: When is the animated form called a bird?

positions.position: It is called a bird once it has living flesh and blood.
positions.reasons: Jishumī favors Abū Hāshim against Abū ʿAlī; the change from clay likeness to living bird is his evidence.

turns_on: The clay likeness is distinguished from living flesh and blood.

question: What does 'by God's permission' mean for the miracles?

positions.position: God Himself brings the life or healing into being when Jesus prays or breathes.
positions.reasons: Rāzī cites 3:145, 67:2 and 2:258; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Ṭabrisī say God originates life, while Jesus visibly shapes and supplicates. Al-Ālūsī says any breath could be its occasion by divine will.

positions.position: God authorizes and enables the act, knowing it will occur.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya compares 2:251 and the report on silence as consent; Abū Ḥayyān combines enabling and knowledge.

positions.position: It means God's command or power.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabrisī and al-Nasafī use command; al-Ṭabrisī distinguishes human shaping and breathing from divine creation of living flesh.

turns_on: Whether permission is knowledge and enabling, command, or God's creating the result.

question: Why is 'by God's permission' repeated and placed after bird-making and resurrection?

positions.position: The repetition attributes astonishing life-giving acts to God and prevents deifying Jesus.
positions.reasons: Al-Kashshāf, Rāzī, Bayḍāwī, al-Biqāʿī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and others explicitly counter claims of Jesus's divinity; al-Biqāʿī compares Adam's dust creation.

positions.position: The phrase is stated after the two greatest miracles; coordination extends its force to healing and foretelling.
positions.reasons: Abū Ḥayyān says creation and resurrection are greatest and the others attach to them; al-Samīn stresses the qualifier after creation and revival.

positions.position: Knowledge and healing omit the phrase because Jesus performs the speech or the healing is already framed as God's sign.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes the spoken report from acts God truly creates, cites 13:38, and says explicit sign language suffices for healing.

turns_on: Avoiding deification; whether omission after healing and knowledge is coordinated scope or a meaningful distinction.

question: What does 'by God's permission' attach to in the bird clause?

positions.position: It modifies yakūn, the bird's becoming.
positions.reasons: Abū Ḥayyān and Abū al-Baqāʾ permit this; al-Samīn says it is clearest if kāna is complete.

positions.position: It modifies ṭayran or ṭāʾiran, describing the bird as enabled by God.
positions.reasons: Al-Samīn allows an omitted relation with collective ṭayr and direct modification of singular ṭāʾiran; Abū Ḥayyān permits this too.

turns_on: Whether the phrase modifies being, the bird description, or the whole miracle.

question: What does 'I heal' mean, and how is the verb formed?

positions.position: Jesus removes illness and restores a patient to health.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī cites Arabic usage for both recovery forms; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says a patient is healed and another heals him; al-Ḥarālī describes full release from impaired faculties.

positions.position: Tamīm uses bariʾtu and Ḥijāz uses baraʾtu.
positions.reasons: Al-Aṣmaʿī gives this attribution; al-Rāghib extends both vowels to illness while debt and sin take fatḥa.

positions.position: The regional attribution is reversed for baraʾtu.
positions.reasons: Abū Zayd says the rest of the Arabs use bariʾtu.

turns_on: The sources vary dialect attributions for bariʾa and baraʾa.

question: How did Jesus treat the crowds of sick people, according to reports?

positions.position: As many as fifty thousand came in a day; he went to those unable to reach him and healed by prayer, often conditional on faith.
positions.reasons: Wahb is repeatedly cited; versions vary on whether he also touched patients. Al-Bursawī reports some believed and others called it magic; al-Ālūsī quotes the prayer and a use for fear or mental illness.

positions.position: Galen and colleagues held congenital blindness and advanced baras incurable.
positions.reasons: Al-Bursawī reports their medical judgment; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān repeat a historical story that Galen died traveling to meet Jesus.

question: Who is al-akmah?

positions.position: A person born blind, often described as never seeing light or having closed/erased eyes.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda recur; Ruʾba and Suwayd are cited for blindness. Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefer this because ordinary treatment cannot restore congenital sight, making the sign conclusive; Ibn Kathīr agrees.

positions.position: A blind person generally, whether born blind or losing sight later.
positions.reasons: Qatāda, al-Ḥasan, al-Suddī and others give the broad gloss; al-Khalīl and al-Rāghib allow acquired blindness. Al-Ṭabarī cites Suwayd and Ruʾba; Ibn ʿĀshūr allows both.

positions.position: A person who sees by day but not at night.
positions.reasons: Mujāhid is the repeated authority, with al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ikrima and al-Aʿmash in some sources. Al-Ṭabarī rejects this because it is medically treatable and not an unanswerable sign.

positions.position: A person with weak, dim, or bleary sight.
positions.reasons: Ikrima is the main reported authority; al-Ṭabarī rejects it as medically treatable. Qirāʾāt and modern summaries call it a minority gloss.

positions.position: A person whose eye was erased or who had no eyeball.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās is cited by al-Ālūsī; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāghib and Bayḍāwī allow effaced eyes. Some report Qatāda b. Diʿāma as the only such person in the Muslim community.

positions.position: A mute, uncomprehending person with a dead heart.
positions.reasons: Al-Naqqāsh gives this figurative view. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says it would be a good proof were it not for the linguistic constraint of blindness.

positions.position: Other reported possibilities include sight only at night or squinting.
positions.reasons: Ibn Kathīr lists these among unspecified glosses while preferring congenital blindness.

turns_on: The decisive issue is whether the word indicates congenital or absolute blindness, lesser sight loss, or a figurative incapacity.

question: What grammatical form links al-akmah and al-abraṣ?

positions.position: Both are afʿal adjectives for defects or disease, whose feminine is faʿlāʾ.
positions.reasons: Sībawayh distinguishes afʿal color and defect patterns, their verbs and verbal nouns, and examples such as aʿwar/ʿawrāʾ; he notes irregular amyal and other neighboring patterns.

question: Why are blindness and al-abraṣ singled out for healing?

positions.position: They resisted physicians, so the cures were a decisive miracle in an age skilled at medicine.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī contrasts curable weak sight; Ibn ʿAṭiyya mentions humoral theory. Many compare Moses' magic and Muḥammad's eloquence. Ibn ʿĀshūr notes Jewish and Arab stigma and Torah isolation of lepers.

positions.position: The named cures do not exclude Jesus healing other ailments.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī notes additional reports; Wahb says thousands gathered, including infirm and mentally ill.

question: What affliction does al-abraṣ denote?

positions.position: A person with baras: white patches or discoloration of the skin.
positions.reasons: Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Samīn and others call it al-waḍaḥ; Arabic uses related names for a white lizard and the moon. Al-Rāghib's claim about the moon's spot is disputed.

positions.position: It is leprosy or an incipient form of it.
positions.reasons: Kur'an Yolu prefers this from al-Bustānī's dictionary material and historical context; Study Quran describes contagion, nerve damage and long incurability.

turns_on: Whether the white patch disease is described as baras/vitiligo or leprosy and its onset.

question: What legal implication is drawn from leprosy?

positions.position: Some Muslim jurists counted baras as a spousal defect permitting annulment, though descriptions were imprecise.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr notes this alongside the disease's stigma.

question: What does Jesus's 'I revive the dead' mean, and who performs it?

positions.position: God literally revived dead persons in answer to Jesus's prayer; the plural suggests several.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī, Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī attribute life to God; Dāmghānī says it preceded final resurrection without lasting worldly sustenance; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites a Gospel girl. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the plural and unqualified promise indicate actual acts.

positions.position: It means spiritual revival of ignorance or dead hearts.
positions.reasons: Al-Qāshānī reads it as imparting knowledge; Asad regards metaphorical renewal as probable, citing 6:122. Ibn al-Jawzī reports restoring the departed soul as another lexical sense.

positions.position: The verse merely offers a possible sign if demanded; occurrence is not established.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports and rejects this view because the wording lacks a conditional such as 'if you asked'.

turns_on: Literal temporary revival by God's answer to prayer versus inward revival of the spiritually dead.

question: How did Jesus raise the dead according to reports, and how reliable are the reports?

positions.position: He prayed to God, sometimes invoking 'O Living, O Sustainer' or the greatest name.
positions.reasons: Al-Kalbī and others give yā ḥayyu yā qayyūm; Sam's revival is linked to the greatest name. Al-Ṭabarī emphasizes answered supplication.

positions.position: A report says he struck a body, grave, or skull with his staff and the dead person spoke.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya gives no authority; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī repeat it, sometimes adding a quick return to death.

positions.position: A report says he prayed two cycles, recited al-Mulk and al-Sajda, and invoked seven names.
positions.reasons: The report is transmitted by Ismāʿīl b. ʿAyyāsh; al-Bayhaqī says its chain is not strong.

positions.position: The individual resurrection narratives are too weak to establish as authentic.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya expressly says this; Abū Ḥayyān leaves the many stories to God's knowledge.

turns_on: Prayer formulas and actions differ; two prayer-cycle report is judged weak.

question: Whom did Jesus revive in the reports?

positions.position: Sām son of Noah rose gray-haired, spoke, then died again.
positions.reasons: Accounts vary on the divine name invoked, how long he had been dead, and whether half his hair whitened from fearing the Hour. Some believed; others called it magic.

positions.position: A widow's or old woman's son rose from a bier and lived.
positions.reasons: Reports add that he dressed, carried the bier home, and later had children.

positions.position: Four are named: Lazarus or al-ʿĀdhir, a widow's son, a tax collector's daughter, and Sām son of Noah.
positions.reasons: The main reports say the first three lived and had children, while Sām returned to death. Jishumī's fourth is instead called the tenth's son; Ibn ʿAbbās and the exegetes recur. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says many reports are unverified.

positions.position: Lazarus, Jesus's friend, rose after three days and later had a child.
positions.reasons: Several reports call him Azar or al-ʿĀdhir; this is a name variant of the same account.

positions.position: A tax collector's daughter, recently dead, rose and later had a child.
positions.reasons: Some call her a girl dead since the previous day; Ibn ʿĀshūr separately cites a Gospel girl just after death.

positions.position: A revived person soon died again.
positions.reasons: Dāmghānī says Sām returned to death; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān report conflicting accounts about duration.

positions.position: Further reports add a king's son, an ancient ʿĀd man in al-Andalus, and a fawn, sheep, and cow.
positions.reasons: Al-Zuhrī tells the al-Andalus account; al-Ālūsī lists additional cases and says the verse's plural embraces them.

turns_on: Different named people, count, and later survival.

question: What does 'I inform you' promise?

positions.position: Jesus discloses concealed facts about their food and stores, without witnessing them.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī, al-Biqāʿī and Ibn ʿĀshūr stress the concealed nature of household facts; al-Kalbī says people challenged him after other miracles. The reports differ on prior night, present day, midday/evening and future meals.

positions.position: Eating means desires or worldly enjoyment; stores mean inward motives or deeds for the next life.
positions.reasons: Al-Qāshānī reads inner appetites and intentions; Asad takes good things enjoyed now and good deeds accumulated for the hereafter.

turns_on: Literal hidden household facts versus inward meanings of consumption and storage.

question: When and in what setting did the disclosure occur?

positions.position: It began while Jesus played or studied with children.
positions.reasons: Al-Suddī, Saʿīd, Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ and Ibn Isḥāq recur; Jesus anticipated lessons and named hidden food or fathers' deeds; parents called him a sorcerer.

positions.position: It occurred when the heavenly table descended and people hid forbidden leftovers.
positions.reasons: Qatāda and ʿAmmār supply the command not to save any for tomorrow; Jesus exposed breach of the covenant.

positions.position: After Jesus raised the dead, people asked for a new sign about their meals and stores.
positions.reasons: Al-Kalbī and later narrations say they first called resurrection magic; Jesus then disclosed midday and evening meals.

positions.position: Both the childhood and table episodes may have occurred.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī explicitly allows both while treating the literal two household facts as the verse's apparent sense.

turns_on: Childhood school, a later challenge, or the heavenly table.

question: What happened to the hidden schoolboys or disobedient eaters in the reports?

positions.position: Parents hid the boys, and Jesus said they would become pigs; they did.
positions.reasons: Al-Suddī says the boys were hidden while their parents lied and called Jesus a sorcerer; Mary fled toward Egypt afterward. Some versions say parents called the boys pigs before Jesus confirmed it.

positions.position: They became apes and pigs after Jesus's prayer or after violating the table command.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAmr's schoolboy report and ʿAmmār's table report give the pair; the latter links fear and betrayal to 5:115.

turns_on: Accounts differ over pigs alone versus apes and pigs, and whether boys or table followers were transformed.

question: Why is the disclosure a prophetic sign rather than ordinary divination?

positions.position: Jesus receives sure unseen knowledge directly from God, without instruments or trickery.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī contrasts astrologers' tools and spirit helpers; Rāzī says astrologers need questions and err. Al-Ālūsī distinguishes jafr and astrology as inference or probability, whereas revelation and inspiration are bestowed.

positions.position: The disclosed fact can be humanly discoverable in principle, but the prophet obtains it by an inaccessible means.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī says a proof need not involve logically unreachable facts; no stratagem explains this disclosure.

positions.position: Joseph's foretelling of food may be a comparable prophetic sign.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reads 'its interpretation' in Joseph's story as referring to the food before arrival, supported by some Imāmī reports.

turns_on: Direct divine disclosure versus inference from instruments, helpers or prior questions.

question: Which food and stores does Jesus identify?

positions.position: Their ordinary household meals and what they saved for later.
positions.reasons: Mujāhid and al-Rabīʿ specify last night's meal; al-Wāḥidī and others morning food and what remained for evening; al-Ḥasan adds fear of not receiving replacement.

positions.position: Food taken from the heavenly table, especially what they were forbidden to save.
positions.reasons: Qatāda and ʿAmmār connect it to the table; disobedient eaters hoarded food and were transformed, with 5:115 cited.

positions.position: Specific personal facts stand for all kinds of unseen information.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī reports this extension; he also says nourishment and reserves command attention and are easily checked.

turns_on: Ordinary household provisions versus food from the heavenly table.

question: How does mā work in 'what you eat and what you store'?

positions.position: Both instances are relative pronouns: the things eaten and stored.
positions.reasons: Al-Zajjāj, al-Ṭabrisī and Abū Ḥayyān prefer this; the omitted resumptive pronouns are understood.

positions.position: Both can be verbal-noun particles: your eating and storing.
positions.reasons: Al-Naḥḥās, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Samīn allow this; most grammarians say this option requires no resumptive pronoun.

positions.position: Both can be indefinite nouns with following adjectival clauses.
positions.reasons: Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī allow this, with an omitted resumptive pronoun.

turns_on: Relative noun, verbal-noun particle, or indefinite noun described by a clause.

question: What does 'you store' mean?

positions.position: You hide or retain something for a later need, especially food.
positions.reasons: Muqātil glosses next-day savings; Jishumī gives future need; al-Ḥarālī distinguishes private storing from ihtikār for trade profit. Al-Samīn cites poetry where dhukhr denotes the thing stored.

question: How is taddakhirūn formed, and how is it read?

positions.position: The common taddakhirūn has doubled dāl from iftiʿāl of dhakhara.
positions.reasons: Al-Farrāʾ, al-Zajjāj, al-Khalīl, Sībawayh and later grammarians explain voicing t to d beside voiced dhāl and assimilation. Al-Naḥḥās prefers this to al-Farrāʾ's reverse account; parallels include izdajara, iḍṭarra, iṣṭabara and Zuhayr's ẓ/ṭ line.

positions.position: A light tadhkharūn uses the simple verb dhakhara, without doubling.
positions.reasons: Al-Farrāʾ reports it; Mujāhid, al-Zuhrī, Ayyūb and Abū al-Sammāl are named. Al-Zajjāj answers an objection of ambiguity.

positions.position: Another assimilation yields doubled dhāl or tadhakhirūn.
positions.reasons: Al-Farrāʾ describes speakers who let dhāl dominate; al-Zajjāj reports dāl/dhāl alternatives; Abū Ḥayyān allows this though favoring the majority.

positions.position: A less assimilated tadhdakhirūn keeps dhāl before dāl.
positions.reasons: Abū Shuʿayb al-Sūsī is cited; al-Samīn calls it permissible but says assimilation is more eloquent.

positions.position: One variant replaces second-person tāʾ with third-person yāʾ.
positions.reasons: Jishumī attributes it to Mujāhid; the ordinary reading addresses 'you'.

turns_on: Assimilated dāl, simple dhāl, doubled dhāl, and unassimilated dhāl-dāl.

question: Why mention the house and what does 'in your houses' attach to?

positions.position: It attaches to 'you store' and locates what they hid privately.
positions.reasons: Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī attach it to the latter verb, with no competing governance; al-Biqāʿī says a house is the most concealing personal place.

question: How is buyūtikum vocalized?

positions.position: The base reading has ḍamma on bāʾ, buyūtikum.
positions.reasons: Qirāʾāt ER calls this canonical base.

positions.position: A dialectal variant has kasra, biyūtikum.
positions.reasons: Qirāʾāt ER says the vowel shift leaves meaning unchanged.

turns_on: Ḍamma versus kasra on bāʾ.

question: Who speaks the closing statement?

positions.position: It continues Jesus's speech to the Israelites.
positions.reasons: Abū Ḥayyān prefers this because the clause is enclosed by Jesus's words; al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī allow it.

positions.position: It is God's independent statement, reporting the proof and rebuking deniers.
positions.reasons: Abū Ḥayyān reports the rebuke analysis; al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī also allow God as speaker.

turns_on: Jesus's continuous speech versus God's independent rebuke.

question: How is the hamza in the closing inna read?

positions.position: It has kasra, opening an independent assertion.
positions.reasons: Abū Mālik specifies kasra and adds an unexplained 'if not' phrase.

question: What does 'that' refer to in the closing statement?

positions.position: All the preceding miracles, taken collectively as one set of signs.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn list bird-making, healing, revival and disclosure; Abū Mālik glosses 'that' as 'this'.

question: How does 'if you are believers' qualify the sign?

positions.position: The sign benefits those who believe or are receptive; disbelief blocks benefit, not its status as a sign.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabrisī says knowledge of God as sender precedes recognizing the messenger; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the signs remain signs either way. Al-Samīn supplies an omitted result: they benefit and reflect.

positions.position: It exhorts people who already claim to believe to act as true believers.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya compares an exhortation 'if you are truly a man'; Abū Ḥayyān compares a son told to obey; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls for sincerity.

turns_on: Future believers benefit, or existing believers are exhorted to sincerity and action.

question: What does 'believers' mean in the final condition?

positions.position: Those who affirm the truth of God's messenger and accept his proof.
positions.reasons: Saʿīd b. Jubayr glosses them as truth-affirmers; Muqātil says assent to Jesus's messengership.

question: How do inward readings understand Jesus's signs?

positions.position: The signs describe spiritual training: clay is an unformed soul, the bird its aspiration, breath divine knowledge, and cures purification.
positions.reasons: Al-Qāshānī addresses prepared descendants of Jacob, reads blind as veiled, leprous as stained by vice and desire, and resurrection as knowledge. Asad reads a destiny shaped from humble lives and faith, with spiritual healing and reviving.

positions.position: A person effaced in self and sustained by lordly attributes gives life only through God.
positions.reasons: Al-Sulamī reports this obscure gloss and immediately stresses that miracles occur by God's leave through bodily instruments.

turns_on: Literal acts versus spiritual education and regeneration.

question: What do adjacent notes say God taught Jesus as Book and wisdom?

positions.position: Book may mean handwriting; a report assigns Jesus nine of ten parts of writing.
positions.reasons: Ibn Jurayj gives writing by hand; Jishumī reports the numerical division without a named authority.

positions.position: Book may be another scripture besides Torah and Gospel, such as Psalms.
positions.reasons: Abū ʿAlī prefers this as closer to the wording and prophethood.

positions.position: Wisdom is knowledge or soundness of speech and action, including prophetic knowledge.
positions.reasons: Jishumī reports both glosses and says Jesus knew Torah, Gospel and wisdom.

turns_on: Writing, another scripture, or broader knowledge and sound action.

question: How does this verse join the account of Mary and Jesus?

positions.position: Mary's birth story pauses; the commentary turns to Jesus's mission, with the remainder of Mary's story in Sūrat Maryam.
positions.reasons: Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī give this narrative division.

positions.position: The angelic promise was certain and fulfilled in Jesus's whole mission.
positions.reasons: Elmalılı cites God's unbroken promise, the angels' truth, minhu and 'Be'; Jesus's life expressed the announced identity and call.

question: Why did Jesus's signs match medicine, and how do other prophets' signs compare?

positions.position: God challenged each audience in its leading skill: Jesus's medicine, Moses's magic, Muḥammad's eloquence.
positions.reasons: Jishumī says a miracle is conclusive when it defeats experts in their own field; Ibn Kathīr adds the Qur'an's inimitability before humans and jinn.

positions.position: Moses's confrontation of Pharaoh and Jesus's Israelite challenge used visible signs before or apart from a new scripture.
positions.reasons: Al-Sāmarrāʾī notes Moses's tablets came after Egypt, so the staff and hand answered Pharaoh; Jesus likewise came with signs.

question: How does the verse answer later claims about Jesus?

positions.position: His miracles and teaching point to worship of God alone, opposing a claim that Jesus or Mary is divine.
positions.reasons: Elmalılı says the whole mission called people to fear and obey their shared Lord; Kur'an Yolu reads the address for Najrān and cites 5:110–118; Ibn ʿĀshūr reports Najrān Christians argued from miracles.

question: What additional signs and stories are attached to Jesus's mission?

positions.position: Reports add garments in requested colors and a royal bowl that did not diminish, gaining disciples.
positions.reasons: Al-Thaʿlabī narrates both, with a disciple identifying divine origin in the cloth sign.

positions.position: Reports also attribute revival and healing signs to others by God's leave.
positions.reasons: Al-Biqāʿī cites 2:260, the Prophet restoring Qatāda's eye and Uways's cured baras, and a report of the Prophet calling a dead daughter. The reports have no grading there.

positions.position: A moral story tells of three men dying through murder and poisoned food over money.
positions.reasons: Al-Durr gives the continuation without named attribution; Khalid al-Ḥadhdhāʾ separately recounts Jesus instructing messengers sent to raise the dead.

question: What do surrounding reports say about the disciples and Jesus's fate?

positions.position: The disciples were called ḥawāriyyūn for laundering and whitening clothes.
positions.reasons: Al-Riḍā reports the popular explanation and a link to ḥiwār bread.

positions.position: They were sincere and purified others from sin through exhortation.
positions.reasons: Al-Riḍā favors this Imāmī interpretation and reports twelve disciples, Luke being most knowledgeable.

positions.position: A report says Jews claimed to torture, kill and crucify Jesus, though God gave them no actual power over him.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṣādiq says it only appeared so; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī glosses a related transformation into devils as affecting a wicked subgroup.

turns_on: Etymology of ḥawāriyyūn and later accounts differ.

question: How can someone receive angelic communication without being a prophet?

positions.position: A muhaddath hears an angel with the heart while remaining distinct from a prophet or messenger.
positions.reasons: Reports name ʿAlī and Salmān; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the hearing is real to the recipient, whose divinely granted knowledge is immediate and certain. He describes prophetic dreaming as a swoon-like perception.

positions.position: Divine light and inward calm distinguish angelic speech from Satanic suggestion.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī links God's light to 6:122 and calm to remembrance at 13:28, while Satanic prompting causes agitation.

question: Must a recipient of angelic communication see an angel?

positions.position: Sight is not required, though an angel may appear in human form.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites Mary's encounter at 19:17–19 and Abraham's household at 11:69–73.

positions.position: Denied vision may mean seeing an angel's actual essence rather than its appearance.
positions.reasons: A proposed reconciliation; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī observes the cited verses establish appearances only.

positions.position: Denied vision may apply specifically to legislative revelation.
positions.reasons: Another proposal preserves the lawgiving role of prophets; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī considers it somewhat remote.

turns_on: Reports deny a requirement; proposed limits concern essence or lawgiving revelation.

question: What broader stylistic points do sources draw from this passage?

positions.position: Shortening a verb can imply only part of an action.
positions.reasons: Al-Sāmarrāʾī gives this rule in two discussions; he compares easier yafʿal for ordinary conception with harder yakhluq for Jesus's fatherless birth.

positions.position: Qur'anic cadence here is not ordinary sajʿ, despite surface resemblance.
positions.reasons: Al-Bāqillānī argues familiar sajʿ could not have baffled hearers or supported the challenge; unbalanced cadence would be disorder, impossible of Qur'anic eloquence.

positions.position: The passage repeats key phrases, uses singular for a collective, and juxtaposes opposites.
positions.reasons: Abū Ḥayyān lists repeated 'I came', bird, permission, Lord and mā; he notes collective singulars and antithesis between life and death and later lawful/forbidden.

positions.position: True synonyms within a single speaker's language are doubtful; variant forms may come from dialect contact.
positions.reasons: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ endorses this; Ibn Jinnī says rarer synonyms may be borrowed tribal forms.

turns_on: Whether its cadence is conventional sajʿ, plus repetition, collective singulars, antithesis and verb shortening.

question: What related grammatical examples do the notes cite outside this wording?

positions.position: Fa-idhā in a related example is a place adverb or particle with an omitted predicate; a time adverb cannot predicate of a person.
positions.reasons: Al-Burhān uses this as a syntactic illustration.

positions.position: A future circumstantial state is allowed when its future sense is clear.
positions.reasons: Al-Samīn compares a falcon example and 39:73, though the normal circumstance is simultaneous.

question: How is this verse linked to other Qur'anic narratives?

positions.position: The miracles recur in 5:110, with further Gospel or Qur'anic comparisons.
positions.reasons: Study Quran notes 5:110 and says the clay bird is absent from the New Testament; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites Matthew 17's Moses and Elijah scene. Al-Qushayrī says Muḥammad knows the prior account by revelation, not inference.

positions.position: Jesus's signs led toward one message: worship of God alone and the straight path.
positions.reasons: Elmalılı treats all miracles as one call, linking the following verse.

question: Did Jesus actually perform the listed signs?

positions.position: The verses present accomplished acts, not hypothetical capabilities.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says hypothetical performance would require an 'if you asked' condition; Jishumī and Elmalılı assert miracles occurred.

positions.position: The verse only states Jesus could perform them if requested.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports and rejects this limitation.

turns_on: Actual acts versus a merely hypothetical offer.
